Taiwanese beauty snake (Orthriophis taeniurus friesei), hence the "One of my beauties" in the title. Best personality in a snake I've ever owned. Among my other snakes she's considered the family pet, my kids love her, my 3 1/2 yr old will walk around with her around his shoulders. Never bit, never hissed, never panicked, never "s" upped. She's just about 6' (1.83 meters) long now, hopefully still growing. What kind of snakes do you keep?

Right now I only have 1 corn snake, but I'm just getting back into keeping reptiles and hopefully get into the world of breeding next year. I can't wait to get more, just working on saving up for a decent rack right now.

Why not a diy rack? I've seen plenty of great diy ones at a fraction the cost of pro racks. Even semi-diy racks, starting out with an ikea/craigslist table/hutch/cabinet and working from there. Diy flexwatt setups are cheap, the sterilite bins aren't that expensive either. Your big expenditure is the temperature controller and time.

Well that still cost money haha, but that is what I plan to do. I just want to make sure I'm doing it all right and not cheaping out on silly things. Even tho I want to do a DIY rack I feel it should still be built just as good as a professional one. I hope to build 6-8 tier rack for more corn and rat snakes first, then branch out to the more exotic snakes like your little beauty there.

Just remember that some snakes fare much better in racks than others. Corns do really well as they're nocturnal, terrestrial, and prefer small dark places to remain most of the time. While my beauty snake is diurnal, semi-arboreal, and without nearly nightly handling they get wicked mean and require quite a large enclosure. She's in a base 125 gallon tank with a comparable sized hood with windows on it, something along the lines of 6'x4'x2' total and she uses it all. If you're plan is to only breed them and not interact with them then they might be fine in a rack, but you won't be able to handle them at all without a hook and no free handling.

Corns might be a better bet overall in a rack system and you can go a month without more than cleaning/feeding for interaction and they're still fine. Profitability wise corns are again probably a better bet too, throw together a bunch of 3+ gene adults and see what hatches, you might end up with something worth quite a bit. Beauty snakes, outside of chinese, essentially have no morphs (except albino) and the morphs present probably have been introduced via chinese beauties. If you see something like a calico blue beauty, that's probably 50% blue / 50% chinese calico. Most people frown on integrades even in something as close as locality beauty snakes, you're yellowish blue beauty will sell for far less as people will assume it has some other beauty snake mixed in it.

Wow thanks for the tips, i'm still pretty new to snakes so Im still learning. I was more of a turtle keeper growing up, but I just don't have the space required for most of there set ups. And after reading this I'll probably just stick with corns for now, and just keep researching other species till I find the ones for me. I was thinking about getting some House snakes as well, I've read they are pretty docile and easy to handle.

Lamprophis fuliginosus are super easy to keep, their diet is simple, and they're really laid back snakes. You'll probably not find other kinds of house snakes for sale, and the other kinds are much tougher not just to find but to keep as they all require something odd, be it diet, humidity, etc. But L. fuliginosus are great for racks, hell, shoe boxes work for them. There's a couple things to watch out for though, they have a tendency to eat their substrate (on accident), so newspaper is probably best, and they require a moist hide when they blue. They hit hard when feeding so you have to use tongs or you might get bit on accident. Other than that, house snakes kick ass. I don't know why they aren't super popular like corns. They're as handleable or maybe even more so than corns, really a friendly snake.

I am making this thread so that we may bring forward common misconceptions on Stoicism, and give explanations on how they are incorrect. This can prove useful in that this thread may be referenced via online links, or the explanations within can provide others with the appropriate diction, phrasing, and explanations in the refutation of misinterpretations elsewhere.

I am not listing all of the misconceptions here myself, but rather asking that you, viewers and subscribers, bring them forward individually, whether it be asking or answering.

One of the largest misconceptions is that Stoicism teaches and advocates for submission and compliance. This is most certainly not the case. Acceptance, or emotional neutrality, is appropriate when one genuinely cannot have any impact on the event in question. Inaction is not appropriate when one may be able to affect a situation for the better, or when an unfortunate result has already occurred, and cannot be undone.

In the event of an undesirable/harmful/consequential occurrence, if there exists a course of action that can be taken to lessen the consequence, it may very well be an appropriate reaction. It is the hosting of one's own useless or debilitating emotions that is frowned upon. More often than not, emotions such as sadness or anger, and whims based on such (vengeance, lethargy, etc) are of no practical use, and only serve to worsen a situation, or one's own happiness and clarity of mind. Composure and clear reasoning are more beneficial to the person and the event than volatile emotion could ever hope to be.

Stoicism does not advocate inaction when one has potential control over a situation. It advocates acceptance, and control of one's own emotions, when the user does not have control. If anybody has any corrections for how I explained the error of this misconception, please feel free to present them to me.
